# Probing the untuned model on ConvFinQA {#sec-probing} **You will learn:** - how the untuned model fails when asked for a DSL program, with and without examples in the prompt; - how to read a model's surprise at each token of the gold answer, and what that has to do with the loss; - the number fine-tuning starts from: the model's mean loss on the gold programs of the validation split. The earlier chapters used one conversation. Here we look at a sample of them. The model is `Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507`, untuned, and every example comes from the **validation split**, never from dev. ## The validation split `train.json` has 3,037 conversations. We hold out a tenth of them for tuning decisions (which prompt, which checkpoint) and train on the rest. The split is made **by report page**: several conversations are written from the same page, and if one were in training and its sibling in validation, the model could be graded on a page it had been trained on. Dev stays untouched, for the final numbers. ::: {#89f644da .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from convfinqa import data from convfinqa.artifacts import get, artifact split = get("train_val_split") fit = list(split.jsonl("train_fit.jsonl")) val = list(split.jsonl("val.jsonl")) pages = lambda convs: {data.page_group(c["id"]) for c in convs} n_turns = lambda convs: sum(len(c["annotation"]["dialogue_break"]) for c in convs) print( f"train-fit: {len(fit):,} conversations, {n_turns(fit):,} turns, " f"{len(pages(fit)):,} pages" ) print( f"val: {len(val):,} conversations, {n_turns(val):,} turns, " f"{len(pages(val)):,} pages" ) assert not pages(fit) & pages(val) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` train-fit: 2,731 conversations, 9,979 turns, 1,429 pages val: 306 conversations, 1,125 turns, 159 pages ``` ::: ::: The split is deterministic (pages are drawn with seed 0), and it is saved as the artifact `train_val_split`, so later chapters read exactly these files. ## Asking the untuned model We take 20 validation conversations at random and ask the model for every turn. Each turn is a separate request with the **gold history** (the earlier answers are the dataset's programs), so the requests are independent and each one measures a single turn. Decoding is greedy and the answer is judged exactly as generated: no cleaning, and an answer the executor rejects is wrong. That is the rule the headline evaluation will use. We try two prompts. **Zero-shot** is the system prompt `Answer with a program in the ConvFinQA DSL.`, the page and the question, and nothing else. **Few-shot** puts two complete conversations, with their gold programs, in front of the same request, drawn from train-fit. These runs take a few minutes (they load the 4B model and generate 68 answers twice), so they are an artifact: built once in a subprocess, and loaded here. The same artifact holds the gold programs' token probabilities that we read in the next section. ::: {#f5cabeae .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} #HEAVY @artifact("probe_val_sample", deps=["train_val_split"], heavy=True) def build_probe_val_sample(out, deps): import json import random import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer from convfinqa.probing import probe_sample name = "Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507" tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( name, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda" ).eval() fit = list(deps["train_val_split"].jsonl("train_fit.jsonl")) val = list(deps["train_val_split"].jsonl("val.jsonl")) rng = random.Random(0) sample = rng.sample(val, 20) shots = rng.sample(fit, 2) result = probe_sample(model, tok, sample, shots) for key, rows in result.items(): (out / f"{key}.jsonl").write_text( "".join(json.dumps(r) + "\n" for r in rows) ) probe = get("probe_val_sample") results = pd.DataFrame(probe.jsonl("answers.jsonl")) surprisal = list(probe.jsonl("surprisal.jsonl")) outputs = results.setting.unique() by_id = {c["id"]: c for c in val} sample = [by_id[s["id"]] for s in surprisal] print(f"{len(results) // len(outputs)} turns from {len(sample)} conversations") results.groupby("setting").kind.value_counts().unstack(0)\ .fillna(0).astype(int).sort_values("few-shot", ascending=False) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 68 turns from 20 conversations ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

What we want here is to **read the failures**. ::: {#52df4692 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} accuracy = results.assign(ok=results.kind == "correct")\ .groupby("setting").ok.mean() print(accuracy.map("{:.0%}".format).to_string()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` setting few-shot 68% zero-shot 24% ``` ::: ::: ### What the failures look like Each kind of failure, with one real output per setting. The gold program is on the right. ``` {.python .cell-code} def show(setting, kind): r = results[(results.setting == setting) & (results.kind == kind)] if r.empty: return r = r.iloc[0] print(f"- **{setting}, `{kind}`**, turn {r.turn + 1} of `{r.id}`\n") print( f" ````\n " + r.output.strip().replace("\n", "\n ")[:400] + "\n ````\n" ) print(f" gold: `{r.gold}`\n") for kind in results.kind.unique(): if kind != "correct": for setting in outputs: show(setting, kind) ``` - **zero-shot, `code_fence`**, turn 1 of `Single_KIM/2008/page_126.pdf-1` ```` To find the difference in income from investment in the retail store leases between 2006 and 2007: - Income in 2006: $1.3 million - Income in 2007: $1.2 million Difference = $1.3 million - $1.2 million = **$0.1 million** ```convfinqa 0.1 ``` ```` gold: `subtract(1.2, 1.3)` - **zero-shot, `syntax`**, turn 3 of `Single_ECL/2017/page_96.pdf-3` ```` The net difference between R&D costs in 2016 and 2015 is: $191 million (2015) - $189 million (2016) = **$2 million** So, the net difference is **$2 million**. ```` gold: `subtract(189, 191)` - **few-shot, `syntax`**, turn 5 of `Single_ECL/2017/page_96.pdf-3` ```` divide(191 - 189, 189) * 100 ```` gold: `subtract(189, 191), divide(#0, 191)` - **zero-shot, `wrong_answer`**, turn 1 of `Single_LMT/2014/page_46.pdf-3` ```` 699 ```` gold: `759` - **few-shot, `wrong_answer`**, turn 3 of `Single_ECL/2017/page_96.pdf-3` ```` subtract(191, 189) ```` gold: `subtract(189, 191)` - **zero-shot, `bad_number`**, turn 3 of `Single_LMT/2014/page_46.pdf-3` ```` The operating profit in 2013 was $759 million, and in 2012 it was $808 million. The change over the year was a decrease of $49 million, or approximately 6%. ```` gold: `subtract(759, 808)` - **few-shot, `bad_number`**, turn 2 of `Single_KIM/2008/page_126.pdf-1` ```` divide(1.2 - 1.3, 1.3) ```` gold: `subtract(1.2, 1.3), divide(#0, 1.3)` - **zero-shot, `wrong_operations`**, turn 3 of `Single_ETR/2008/page_313.pdf-1` ```` -32.1 ```` gold: `subtract(959.2, 991.1)` - **few-shot, `wrong_operations`**, turn 3 of `Double_AES/2018/page_168.pdf` ```` 340 ```` gold: `divide(340, 17%)` - **zero-shot, `unknown_operator`**, turn 2 of `Single_MRO/2008/page_99.pdf-2` ```` average(20000, 15000) ```` gold: `add(20000, 15000), divide(#0, const_2)` - **few-shot, `unknown_operator`**, turn 2 of `Single_MRO/2008/page_99.pdf-2` ```` average(20000, 15000) ```` gold: `add(20000, 15000), divide(#0, const_2)` - **few-shot, `wrong_numbers`**, turn 2 of `Double_AES/2018/page_168.pdf` ```` subtract(348, 352), divide(#0, 364) ```` gold: `subtract(348, 352), divide(#0, 352)` The kinds, as `probing.classify_output` defines them: - `code_fence`: the answer is wrapped in a markdown fence, usually with invented syntax inside. - `syntax`, `bad_number`, `unknown_operator`: the executor could not read it. These are **format failures**: the model answered in some language, but not the DSL. - `wrong_operations`, `wrong_numbers`, `wrong_answer`: a valid program with the wrong answer. These are **reasoning or reading failures**: a different list of operations, different numbers picked from the page, or the right shape with the wrong value. Examples shift the balance from the first group to the second: the model learns the format from two conversations, but picking the right cells and the right operation is a different skill. Fine-tuning has to teach both, and the invalid rate it removes is the easy part. ## How surprised is the model by the gold program? Generation shows what the model does. We can also ask how likely it finds **the gold answer**. One forward pass over the whole conversation gives, for every token, the probability the model assigned to it given everything before it. The negative log of that probability is the token's **surprisal**, in nats (natural log). It is the surprisal of the **gold** token given the **gold** tokens before it (teacher forcing), with no comparison to what the model would have chosen. The cross-entropy loss fine-tuning minimizes is the mean surprisal over the answer tokens. ::: {#e6486edb .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} from IPython.display import HTML from convfinqa.book.viz import surprisal_html row = next( r for r in surprisal if len(by_id[r["id"]]["annotation"]["dialogue_break"]) >= 4 ) conv = by_id[row["id"]] pieces, logp = row["tokens"], row["logprobs"] for k, t in enumerate(data.turns(conv)): print(f"turn {k + 1}: {t.question}") HTML(surprisal_html(pieces, logp)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` turn 1: what were the r&d costs in 2016? turn 2: what were the r&d costs in 2015? turn 3: what is the net difference? turn 4: what were the r&d costs in 2015? turn 5: what was the percent change? ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Hover over a token for its probability. The answers are printed one after the other, each ending with `<|im_end|>`, the token that closes the turn. Red marks a token the model gave less than about 2%. Hover over a token for its probability. The answers are printed one after the other, each ending with `<|im_end|>`, the token that closes the turn. Red marks a token the model gave less than about 2%. The red is not where we might expect. The numbers, which the model has to find on the page, are mostly pale, because it copies them well. The surprise is in the **DSL's own words**: the operator that opens a program, the `),` between two steps, the `(#` of a reference to an earlier step. We can measure it across the sample, by kind of token: ::: {#187f0ddc .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} def token_class(piece): text = piece.strip() if piece == "<|im_end|>": return "end of turn" if "#" in text: return "#k reference" if text.startswith(")") and "," in text: return "step separator" if text.replace("_", "").isalpha(): return "operator / constant name" if text and all(ch.isdigit() or ch in ".%,-" for ch in text): return "number" return "bracket / other" records = [] for row in surprisal: turn = 0 for piece, lp in zip(row["tokens"], row["logprobs"]): records.append({ "class": token_class(piece), "turn": min(turn, 4) + 1, "surprisal": -lp }) turn += piece == "<|im_end|>" tokens = pd.DataFrame(records) by_class = tokens.groupby("class").surprisal.agg(["count", "mean", "sum"]) by_class["share of total"] = by_class["sum"] / by_class["sum"].sum() by_class.drop(columns="sum").sort_values("share of total", ascending=False)\ .round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}

The mean surprisal also falls from turn to turn as earlier answers in the chat show the format, but only a little at first: the model does not pick the format up from one or two answers. Numbers cost little, and what is left for fine-tuning is the **reasoning** that decides the operator and the arguments. ## The number fine-tuning starts from For the whole validation split we compute the mean surprisal of the gold tokens: one forward pass per conversation, token-weighted. This is a model run over 306 conversations, so it is built once as an artifact, in a subprocess. ::: {#8ecdce42 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} #HEAVY @artifact("val_gold_nll", deps=["train_val_split"], heavy=True) def build_val_gold_nll(out, deps): import json import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer from convfinqa.formatting import conversation_messages from convfinqa.probing import mean_gold_nll name = "Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507" tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( name, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda" ).eval() chats = [ conversation_messages(c) for c in deps["train_val_split"].jsonl("val.jsonl") ] (out / "nll.json").write_text(json.dumps(mean_gold_nll(model, tok, chats))) val_nll = get("val_gold_nll").json("nll.json") print( f"val: {val_nll['conversations']} conversations, " f"{val_nll['tokens']:,} answer tokens" ) print( f"mean gold-program negative log-likelihood: " f"{val_nll['nll']:.4f} nats per token" ) from math import exp print(f"perplexity: {exp(val_nll['nll']):.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` val: 306 conversations, 16,417 answer tokens mean gold-program negative log-likelihood: 2.2062 nats per token perplexity: 9.081 ``` ::: ::: The **perplexity** is the exponential of this mean: the model is as uncertain, on average, as if it were choosing uniformly among that many tokens at each gold position. A perplexity of 1 would mean every gold token had probability 1. It is an average of a lopsided distribution (the earlier table shows a few very costly tokens among many nearly free ones), it is per token, so it depends on the tokenizer, and it covers the answer tokens only. It carries the same information as the loss; we report both because the training logs show the loss and the perplexity is easier to picture. The mean negative log-likelihood is the loss of the untuned model on the validation split, with the data in exactly the format the training will use. The training chapter uses the same format, so its **step-0 validation loss** should agree with it within a few percent: if it doesn't, the formatting or the label mask differs between the two, and we look there first. After training we expect the loss to fall, and the same heatmap to be much paler. ::: {.callout-note title="Under the hood"} The loss is a mean over tokens, not over conversations or turns, so long conversations weigh more. `probing.gold_logprobs` scores token `t` with the logits at position `t - 1`, which is how the model's own `labels=` loss is defined; @sec-fine-tuning shows the two agree. Attention maps from a copied number back to table cells are a natural next probe, but they are only suggestive: a head that attends to a cell is not thereby the reason for the answer [@vaswani2017attention]. We leave them out. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Further reading"} - The ConvFinQA paper measured GPT-3 with the same DSL and found the unfamiliar syntax hurt it [@chen2022convfinqa]. :::
